introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 3 (0790), Paper 3 (Critical Thinking), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each section (Section One: Logic; Section Two: Philosophical Problems). Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion, as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**3.** (a) Given that p: "*students work hard*", q: "*the results are good*" and r: "*parents are proud*" symbolise the following statements and represent on truth tables:

(i) If students do not work hard, then it is not the case that the results are good and parents are not proud

(ii) Either students work hard and parents are proud or students do not work hard and parents are not proud

(iii) Students do not work hard and parents are not proud, only if the results are good.

(3x3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (3 marks).** "If students do not work hard (~p), then it is not the case that [the results are good (q) and parents are not proud (~r)]":

$$\sim p \supset \sim(q \cdot \sim r)$$

| $p$ | $q$ | $r$ | $\sim p$ | $\sim r$ | $q \cdot \sim r$ | $\sim(q \cdot \sim r)$ | $\sim p \supset \sim(q \cdot \sim r)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | F | F | T | T |
| T | T | F | F | T | T | F | T |
| T | F | T | F | F | F | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T | F | T | T |
| F | T | T | T | F | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | T | T | F | **F** |
| F | F | T | T | F | F | T | T |
| F | F | F | T | T | F | T | T |

The statement is false only when students do not work hard, the results are good and parents are not proud (a contingent statement).

**(ii) (3 marks).** "Either [students work hard and parents are proud] or [students do not work hard and parents are not proud]":

$$(p \cdot r) \vee (\sim p \cdot \sim r)$$

| $p$ | $q$ | $r$ | $p \cdot r$ | $\sim p \cdot \sim r$ | $(p \cdot r) \vee (\sim p \cdot \sim r)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | F | **T** |
| T | T | F | F | F | F |
| T | F | T | T | F | **T** |
| T | F | F | F | F | F |
| F | T | T | F | F | F |
| F | T | F | F | T | **T** |
| F | F | T | F | F | F |
| F | F | F | F | T | **T** |

The two disjuncts can never be true together, so the inclusive $\vee$ and the "either ... or" give the same result. The column is identical to the truth table of $p \equiv r$ ($q$ plays no part).

**(iii) (3 marks).** "A only if B" is symbolised $A \supset B$. Here A is "students do not work hard and parents are not proud" ($\sim p \cdot \sim r$) and B is "the results are good" ($q$):

$$(\sim p \cdot \sim r) \supset q$$

| $p$ | $q$ | $r$ | $\sim p$ | $\sim r$ | $\sim p \cdot \sim r$ | $(\sim p \cdot \sim r) \supset q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | F | F | T |
| T | T | F | F | T | F | T |
| T | F | T | F | F | F | T |
| T | F | F | F | T | F | T |
| F | T | T | T | F | F | T |
| F | T | F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | F | T | T | T | **F** |

The statement is false only when students do not work hard, parents are not proud and the results are not good.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Determine if the following statement forms are tautologies, contradictions or contingent sentences.

(i) $(\sim A \cdot B) \vee (B \vee A)$

(ii) $(p \cdot q) \supset (q \cdot p)$

(iii) $\sim(p \vee q) \equiv (q \vee p)$

(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (2 marks).** $(\sim A \cdot B) \vee (B \vee A)$

| $A$ | $B$ | $\sim A \cdot B$ | $B \vee A$ | whole |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T |
| F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | F | **F** |

True in three rows and false in one: **contingent**. (The form is equivalent to $A \vee B$.)

**(ii) (2 marks).** $(p \cdot q) \supset (q \cdot p)$

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \cdot q$ | $q \cdot p$ | whole |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T |
| F | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | F | F | T |

True in every row: a **tautology** (the antecedent and consequent are equivalent by commutation).

**(iii) (2 marks).** $\sim(p \vee q) \equiv (q \vee p)$

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \vee q$ | $\sim(p \vee q)$ | $q \vee p$ | whole |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | T | F |
| T | F | T | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | T | F |
| F | F | F | T | F | F |

False in every row: a **contradiction** (the two sides always have opposite truth values).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Test the validity of the following arguments using the short truth table method

(i) $(A \cdot B) \vee (C \cdot D)$

$\sim(A \cdot B)\ /\ \therefore \sim(C \cdot D)$

(ii) $\sim(B \cdot C) \supset \sim(D \cdot E)$

$D \cdot E\ /\ \therefore B \cdot C$

(2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method:** try to make the **conclusion false** and **all premises true**. If this is possible, the argument is invalid; if it forces a contradiction, it is valid.

**(i) (3 marks).** $(A \cdot B) \vee (C \cdot D),\ \sim(A \cdot B)\ /\ \therefore\ \sim(C \cdot D)$

- Make the conclusion false: $\sim(C \cdot D) = F$, so $C \cdot D = T$, hence $C = T$ and $D = T$.
- Make premise 2 true: $\sim(A \cdot B) = T$, so $A \cdot B = F$. Choose $A = F$ (and $B = T$, for example).
- Premise 1: $(A \cdot B) \vee (C \cdot D) = F \vee T = T$. It is true with no further choice.

| $A$ | $B$ | $C$ | $D$ | $(A \cdot B) \vee (C \cdot D)$ | $\sim(A \cdot B)$ | $\sim(C \cdot D)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F | T | T | T | T | T | **F** |

Both premises are true and the conclusion is false: the argument is **invalid**. (The disjunctive syllogism would conclude $C \cdot D$, not $\sim(C \cdot D)$.)

**(ii) (3 marks).** $\sim(B \cdot C) \supset \sim(D \cdot E),\ D \cdot E\ /\ \therefore\ B \cdot C$

- Make the conclusion false: $B \cdot C = F$.
- Make premise 2 true: $D \cdot E = T$, so $D = E = T$.
- Premise 1 then reads $\sim(B \cdot C) \supset \sim(D \cdot E) = T \supset F = F$ (since $\sim(B \cdot C) = T$ and $\sim(D \cdot E) = F$), so premise 1 is false.

It is **impossible** to make the conclusion false and both premises true: the argument is **valid** (it is a modus tollens: $\sim P \supset \sim Q,\ Q\ /\ \therefore\ P$ with $P = B \cdot C$ and $Q = D \cdot E$).
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Using the key provided, symbolise the following:

(i) He who is a thief is a killer. (Tx: x is a thief; Kx: x is a killer)

(ii) Every dog is not a cat. (Dx: x is a dog; Cx: x is a cat)

(2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (2 marks).** "He who is a thief is a killer" is a universal affirmative proposition (A): for every individual $x$, if $x$ is a thief then $x$ is a killer.

$$(x)(Tx \supset Kx)$$

**(ii) (2 marks).** "Every dog is not a cat" means that **no dog is a cat** (universal negative, E): for every $x$, if $x$ is a dog then $x$ is not a cat.

$$(x)(Dx \supset \sim Cx)$$

Equivalent form: $\sim(\exists x)(Dx \cdot Cx)$, "there is no $x$ that is both a dog and a cat".

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR**

(a) (i) What is a valid argument form? State an example. (2 marks)

(ii) State the operative principle behind the affirming and denying modes of the hypothetical syllogism. (3 marks)

(iii) Explain how the principle in a(ii) above works in each case. (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (2 marks).** A **valid argument form** is a pattern of reasoning such that **no argument of that form can have true premises and a false conclusion**: whatever statements are substituted for the variables, if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Validity concerns the form, not the actual truth of the premises.

Example: **modus ponens**, $p \supset q,\ p\ /\ \therefore\ q$. "If it rains, the road is wet. It rains. Therefore the road is wet." (A truth table confirms that the only row where $p \supset q$ and $p$ are both true has $q$ true.)

**(ii) (3 marks).** The affirming mode of the hypothetical syllogism is **modus ponens** (affirming the antecedent, $p \supset q,\ p\ /\ \therefore\ q$) and the denying mode is **modus tollens** (denying the consequent, $p \supset q,\ \sim q\ /\ \therefore\ \sim p$). The operative principle behind both is the relation between the two parts of a conditional: **the antecedent is a sufficient condition of the consequent, and the consequent is a necessary condition of the antecedent.** Hence one may validly **affirm the antecedent** or **deny the consequent**; the reverse moves (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent) are fallacies, because the consequent can be true for other reasons.

**(iii) (2 x 2 marks).**

- *Affirming mode (modus ponens).* Since the antecedent is **sufficient** for the consequent, once the antecedent is given as true the consequent must be true. "If a candidate works hard, he passes; he works hard; so he passes."
- *Denying mode (modus tollens).* Since the consequent is **necessary** for the antecedent, if the consequent is false the antecedent cannot be true (if it were true, the consequent would have to be true, which contradicts the second premise). Example: if a candidate works hard, he passes; he did not pass; so he did not work hard.
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Explain what the following concepts mean

(i) Tautology

(ii) Contingent sentence

(iii) Contradictory sentence

(2x3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Tautology (2 marks).** A statement form that is **true under every assignment of truth values** to its component statements; it is true by its logical form alone and tells us nothing about the world. Example: $p \vee \sim p$ (every row of its truth table is T). Any tautological conditional expresses a valid argument.

**(ii) Contingent sentence (2 marks).** A statement form that is **true under some assignments and false under others**: its truth value depends on the facts, not on the form alone. Example: $p \cdot q$, or $p \supset q$ (both have at least one T row and at least one F row).

**(iii) Contradictory sentence (2 marks).** A statement form that is **false under every assignment** of truth values (a self-contradiction): it cannot be true. Example: $p \cdot \sim p$ (every row of its truth table is F). The negation of a tautology is a contradiction, and the negation of a contradiction is a tautology.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) State the difference between a valid and a sound argument

(ii) In your opinion, which argument has convincing power? Justify your answer

(2x2.5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (2.5 marks).**

- A **valid** argument is one whose **conclusion follows necessarily from its premises**: if the premises were true, the conclusion could not be false. Validity depends only on the form; a valid argument may have false premises and a false conclusion ("All birds are fish; all fish can fly; so all birds can fly").
- A **sound** argument is a valid argument **whose premises are all actually true**; its conclusion is then necessarily true.

So every sound argument is valid, but a valid argument is not necessarily sound. Soundness = validity + true premises.

**(ii) (2.5 marks).** In my opinion the argument with convincing power is the **sound argument**. Justification:

- Validity guarantees that the conclusion follows from the premises, so a rational person who accepts the premises cannot consistently reject the conclusion.
- The truth of the premises guarantees that the conclusion is true in fact, not merely "if" the premises were true. A valid argument with false premises gives no reason to accept its conclusion, and an invalid argument, even with true premises, does not establish its conclusion.
- To convince an audience, the premises must also be accepted or be verifiable by it; a sound argument whose premises are obscure may fail to persuade in practice, but rationally it remains the argument that deserves assent.
themes: rules of inference and argument forms
